scope_gaps.note: The study tested healthy adults aged 21-38 under laboratory conditions with fixed time in bed; the title turns this into general advice to reserve sleep time and not to treat lack of sleepiness as proof of being rested.
The NHS figure sits on an insomnia page and is an average; it is not an individual requirement.

The NHS page is about insomnia and tells readers to see a GP when habit changes have not helped. It does not describe significant daytime sleepiness despite adequate opportunity to sleep as a separate situation, and it says nothing about consulting instead of using more caffeine.

A reader might take 'przez 14 dni' to apply to the total sleep deprivation comparison too; the sentence does not say so, and the abstract describes total deprivation as a separate 3-night experiment. Time in bed was per night.

Result concerns healthy adults aged 21-38 in a laboratory over 14 days with 4 or 6 h time in bed per night; the abstract gives no figures for the size of the deficits or their clinical meaning. The link between sleepiness ratings and unawareness is the authors' interpretation.

Randomization is stated only for the chronic sleep restriction experiment; allocation in the total sleep deprivation experiment is not described in the abstract. The NHS passage is a general statement on an insomnia page.
The NHS says 'on average' and 'everyone needs different amounts'; 'orientacja' and 'indywidualna recepta' are editorial wording, not NHS terms.
The general claim that sleep quality counts is not stated in either snapshot; only symptoms of disrupted sleep are listed by the NHS.
